summary: Jeremiah 15 (21 verses) continues the story of judgment. Starting with 'Then Yahweh said to me, “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind would not turn toward this people. Cast them out of my sight, and let them go out!', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows judgment lived out in jerusalem falling. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Then Yahweh said to me, “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind would not turn toward this people. Cast them out of my sight, and let them go out!
Yahweh said, “Most certainly I will strengthen you for good. Most certainly I will cause the enemy to make supplication to you in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.
“I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem you out of the hand of the terrible.”

questions.question: What is happening in Jeremiah 15?
questions.answer: In 21 verses, this chapter jeremiah 15 (21 verses) continues the story of judgment. starting with 'then yahweh said to me, “though moses and samuel stood before me, yet my mind would not turn toward this people. cast them out of my sight, and let them go out!', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears. The setting is jerusalem falling, written to judah before exile. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Jeremiah and why 15 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally jeremiah, addressed to judah before exile around ~600 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophetic laments — its themes of judgment, new covenant build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'kingdom' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: God's reign/ rule. In this chapter, it appears in context of judgment. For a first-time reader: think of it as god's reign/ rule, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through judgment and new covenant, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 2 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'It will happen when they ask you, ‘Where shall we go out?’ then you shall tell them, ‘Yahweh says: “Such as are for death, to death; such as are for the sword, to the sword; such a...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about judgment. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
